23231-rich-enough: Rich Enough turns on a plain talk about money and family safety. Its speaker wants to secure something for his family in case of accident, investing only what he does not need for daily use, in a way that brings compound interest. He hopes not to touch the interest for years, but to add it to the principal with sums spared from daily work.
antiquities-of-mexico-vol-2-kingsborough:
Lord Kingsborough, an Irish peer named Edward King, poured his fortune into Antiquities of Mexico. Volume Two continues his huge record of Mexican codices. He hired artists to copy the painted books by hand.

The set preserves Aztec and Mixtec images that might else be lost. Kingsborough believed the codices proved grand links between worlds. His obsession cost him his wealth and health. The work is dated in its theories yet vital in its images. Scholars still thank him for saving records of a world Spain tried hard to erase.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardagh:
Ardagh, meaning High Field, is an Irish diocese in the province of Armagh, named for a town in Longford, Leinster. Colgan says Patrick baptized Maine, lord of South Teffia, and built a church at Ardachadh, which remains a see. He consecrated Mel, son of his sister Darerca, as bishop, leaving Mel's brother Melchu as co-bishop. Archbishop Healy accepts this, though Lanigan and O'Hanlon reject a joint episcopate of the brothers.

Founded in 454, Ardagh's church counts among Ireland's most ancient. Mel, also abbot of the adjoining monastery, remains diocesan patron, and outside the town stand ruins of a small primitive church of massive, cyclopean stonework. The see first covered the country of the Eastern Conmaice, the territory of the O'Ferals. The entry weighs rival histories of a see whose origins sit close to Patrick himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armagh:
Armagh, an archdiocese founded by Patrick about 445 as Ireland's primatial and metropolitan see, covers almost all of Armagh and Louth counties. It also covers much of Tyrone, and parts of Derry and Meath. It holds fifty-five parishes, two of them, Armagh and Dundalk, mensal parishes attached to the see. Its chapter, restored in 1856, counted thirteen members in 1906, with 139 clergy, thirty-nine regulars, 156 churches and chapels, 227 primary schools, and a Catholic population of 147,358 in 1901.

Its suffragans are Meath, Ardagh, Clogher, Derry, Down and Connor, Dromore, Kilmore, and Raphoe. Patrick, granted land by the chieftain Daire on Ard-Macha, the Height of Macha, raised a stone church on the summit. With a monastery and other buildings round it, he fixed there his metropolitan seat. The entry joins primatial dignity to parish figures and to a hilltop founding story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-of-p:
Benedict of Peterborough, an abbot and writer, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birthplace and birth date are unknown, and he died in 1193. Educated at Oxford, he served as chancellor to the Archbishop of Canterbury in 1174 and prior of Christ Church, Canterbury, the next year.

As abbot of Peterborough from 1177 until his death, he put the abbey's finances in order and pressed on with building and decoration. Favour with King Richard I won the abbey rights and privileges, and he enriched its library with copied books. The entry warns against confusing him with a namesake bishop of Rochester.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edinburgh:
Scotland's capital, though not its largest city, Edinburgh takes its name from Edwin's burgh, a fortress raised about 620. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places it on a lofty Pentland spur above the Firth of Forth, where Anglian rule in northern Northumbria took hold. Its castle was a royal home under Malcolm Canmore, husband of Saint Margaret, who died there in 1093.

Around the castle the town grew, and below it rose the collegiate church of Saint Giles in the twelfth century. King David the First, Margaret's son, founded Holyrood Abbey at the foot of the castle hill in 1128. For centuries the town stretched no farther than the ridge running east from the castle, and the entry draws on Wilson, Lees, and Arnot for its story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-bradsh:
Edward Bradshaigh was an English Carmelite friar known in religion as Elias of Jesus, born in Lancashire early in the seventeenth century and dead at Benfold in 1652. Fourth son of Roger Bradshaigh of Haigh Hall, he came from a house that gave three sons to the Jesuits and one to the secular clergy. Schooled by Cassinese Benedictines, he joined the Discalced Carmelites in Belgium in 1619.

Sent to England in 1626, he was arrested as a priest, jailed, and freed at the plea of powerful friends, among them the King of Spain, then banished to France. After a spell as reader in Paris he came home to Haigh Hall in 1632, visited the poor, and made converts. Late in life he turned to English antiquities, though his two works on the subject were lost in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-kavana:
Edward Kavanagh was an American statesman and diplomat from Maine, born at Newcastle in 1795 and dead there in 1844. His father came from Ireland in 1780 and grew rich as a merchant and shipowner, while his mother, a Boston native, had turned Catholic. Their home welcomed missionary priests, among them the future Cardinal Cheverus. Young Kavanagh studied at Georgetown and Saint Mary's, Baltimore, then finished his learning in Europe.

Back home he practised law, sat in the Maine legislature from 1826, and served two terms in Congress from 1831. As charge d'affaires at Lisbon from 1835 he settled old claims and won a trade treaty despite revolution and bankruptcy in Portugal. Later he presided over the Maine senate, helped frame the Webster-Ashburton preliminaries, and served nine months as governor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galway-and-ki:
Galway and Kilmacduagh, an Irish diocese of about 250,000 acres, joins two ancient sees in County Galway. Kilmacduagh traces to Saint Colman, a kinsman of King Guaire, who left his hermit cell in the Burren to found a monastery in 610 and became bishop of all Hy Fiachrach. He died in 632. At Kells the see became a suffragan of Tuam.

Later bishops bore old Irish names, from O'Shaughnessy to O'Moloney, while Henry VIII's man Bodkin played courtier to king and queen. Hugh De Burgo fought in the Kilkenny Confederation, then faced Cromwell's exile and confiscation. Kilmacduagh joined Kilfenora in 1750, and Galway town, once a fishing village by the Corrib, grew beside the older monastic world of Annaghdown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-ellis-:
George Ellis Pugh, an Ohio jurist and statesman born at Cincinnati in 1822, rose from the bar to the United States Senate. Educated at Miami University, he joined Ohio's supreme court bar in 1844 and won high repute in Cincinnati practice. He served as a captain in the Mexican War, commended for bravery at Atlixco in 1847. He then sat in Ohio's House, as city solicitor in 1850, and as state attorney-general from 1852 to 1854.

Pugh entered the Senate in December 1855 as the first Ohio native in that body. He worked on public lands and the Judiciary and backed Douglas's popular sovereignty on slavery and the Kansas-Nebraska territories. Chase beat him for re-election in 1861. His noted argument came in 1863, seeking Vallandigham's release from military custody by habeas corpus. He and his wife entered the Church in 1855.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-cavanag:
Soldier James Cavanagh was born in County Tipperary, Ireland, in 1831. He died in New York on 7 January 1901. He emigrated to New York at sixteen and worked as a carpenter. In 1852 he enlisted as a private in the Sixty-Ninth Militia Regiment. He was captain of Company C when it entered Civil War service on 23 April 1861. When the regiment returned after Bull Run, it reorganized as the Sixty-Ninth New York Volunteers of the Irish Brigade. Cavanagh returned to the front as its major.

In that rank he served in Army of the Potomac campaigns until Fredericksburg on 13 December 1862. There he was shot in the hip while leading his regiment up Marye's Heights. He was then discharged for disability from his wound. When the militia reorganized as the National Guard, he rejoined the regiment and rose to lieutenant colonel. The entry presents an Irish Brigade officer of the Civil War.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-of-saru:
Syrian church writer James of Sarugh was called the flute of the Holy Spirit and harp of the believing church. He was born at Kurtam in 451, probably in Sarugh district, to a priest father. He died at Batnan on 29 November 521. Three Syriac biographies survive: one by James of Edessa in the seventh century, one anonymous, and one by George, likely bishop of Sarugh and contemporary of James of Edessa. Where he was educated and when he was ordained priest are unknown.

He became periodeutes, or chorepiscopus, of Haura in Sarugh district. From there in 502 he wrote to Edessa, threatened by Persians, and in 519 to Najran's Christians. In 519 he became bishop of Batnan, Sarugh's chief city. Assemani tried to prove his orthodoxy against Renaudot, but his letters to monks raise doubts. The entry presents a hymn-writer bishop whose theology scholars still debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jedburgh:
Jedburgh, a Scottish Augustinian abbey town in Roxburghshire, took its priory from David I of Scots in 1118, colonised by canons regular from Saint-Quentin at Beauvais. Fordun dates the foundation to 1147, but that year seems to mark its rise from priory to abbey under its first abbot Osbert.

Jedburgh soon ranked among Scotland's great monasteries, favoured by its castle, a favourite royal residence. Gifts of lands, churches, houses, and fisheries from David, Malcolm IV, William the Lion, and others. Alexander III married Yolande de Dreux in its church in 1285, when the great church was likely complete. Border wars later left it uninhabitable about 1300, then plundered and burned at least four times before the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julia-kavanag:
Julia Kavanagh was an Irish novelist and biographer of French life. Born at Thurles in 1824, only child of the poet and philologist Morgan Kavanagh, she grew up largely in France and returned to London in 1844 to write for a living. Her first book, The Three Paths, a children's tale, appeared in 1847.

Madeleine of 1848, drawn from an Auvergne peasant girl, made her name, and her biographies of French and English women of letters showed fine judgment. Her twenty novels, including Nathalie, Daisy Burns, and Rachel Gray, paint French character with quiet, pure prose and high moral tone. She died at Nice in 1877, long devoted to her invalid mother.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-middlesbrough: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Middlesbrough — the Yorkshire diocese. Richard Lacy gives its founding story. Its bishops guard the Tees flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the English north. Its 1878 founding is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peterborough: Peterborough's great abbey church became a cathedral, and its diocese serves Ontario's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the Kawarthas: its noble cathedral serves the Ontario lake country faithfully and well today in 1913.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pittsburgh: Pittsburgh became the diocese of the steel city's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and institutions. The faith in the city of the mills: its noble cathedral crowns the smoky city hilltop high above the meeting rivers of steel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-creag: Richard Creagh was the archbishop of Armagh in the penal years. This entry traces his consecration, his sufferings, and his death. The primate of the hunted church: his long prison held the primate in London's Tower for years of pain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-andrews: St. Andrews and Edinburgh became the archdiocese of Scotland's east. This entry covers its archbishops, its parishes, and its history. The restored hierarchy's primacy: its primatial see crowns the capital of Scotland in Edinburgh's old town today still in the 1900s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schoningh: Schöningh, the name of the Paderborn publishers, carries a Catholic history. This brief entry notes its books and its fame. A quiet name from the German press: its Catholic books served the schools in the 1800s' Germany in Westphalia's towns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-gle: The School of Glendalough was the monastery of the Wicklow hills. This entry covers its founder, its scholars, and its fame. The learning of the two lakes: its holy monks taught Leinster in the 500s' age of the saints in the east.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-colman-of-: St. Colman of Kilmacduagh was the hermit bishop of the Burren. This entry traces his cave, his see, and his cult. The solitary of the Clare hills: his lonely see crowned Kilmacduagh in the 600s' Burren in the west of the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hugh: St. Hugh was the bishop of Lincoln. This long entry examines his charterhouse, his swan, and his fame. The Carthusian of the English see: his tame swan crowned Lincoln in the 1180s' England in the north of the kingdom in the Witham.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-werburgh: St. Werburgh was the abbess princess. This entry traces her Mercia, her Chester, and her cult. The royal nun of the English church: her holy shrine crowned Chester in the 680s' Dee in the river of the city in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-book-of-a: The Book of Armagh is the Irish treasure. This entry traces its Ferdomnach, its Patrick, and its fame. The manuscript of the primatial see: its old vellum crowned Armagh in the 800s of the Vikings in the very old raids.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-school-of: The school of Armagh was the Irish university. This entry traces its Patrick, its scholars, and its fame. The college of the primatial city: its learned scholars crowned Armagh in the 400s of the Patrick in the very old school.
cicero-de-re-publica-featherstonhaugh:
Cicero's On the Republic, written between 54 and 51 BC, imagines Rome's great men debating the best form of state. G. W. Featherstonhaugh's 1829 English translation is the text here, the first made in America. Much of the original was lost for centuries and partly recovered from a Vatican manuscript in 1820.

Scipio Aemilianus leads the talk, praising a mixed state that blends king, nobles, and people in balance. He traces Rome's growth as proof that such a state matures by slow use, not by one man's design. The dialogue closes with the Dream of Scipio, a vision of the heavens and the smallness of earthly fame. The dream was copied and loved all through the Middle Ages.
cicero-friendship-old-age-shuckburgh:
Cicero, Rome's great orator, wrote two short dialogues near the end of his life. Evelyn Shuckburgh translated On Friendship and On Old Age into English. Both works speak through honored older Romans of an earlier generation.

In On Friendship, Laelius praises loyalty between equals bound by virtue and trust. On Old Age gives the aged Cato a calm defense of later life. Cicero argues that age brings counsel, memory, and freedom from appetite. The pair became beloved school texts across Europe for centuries. Their humane, practical tone still suits readers facing retirement or grief today.
doe-osti-17118567-demonstration-of-nekrs: NekRS flow through a squeeze got demoed, and this DOE report covers the contraction demonstration. The pages detail the results for Pronghorn and SAM. The thermal-hydraulics folks get their data. The flow was demonstrated. The data were thermal. The squeeze was contraction.
doe-osti-2998163-addressing-key-physics-: High-energy-density plasmas got their kinetic sims, and this DOE report addresses the key physics. The pages detail the novel capability. The plasma physicists get their tool. The plasmas were HED. The capability was novel. The physicists got tools.
doe-osti-2998949-fem-modeling-and-simula: Nb3Sn wires got their FEM modeling, and this DOE report simulates 2D high specific heat. The pages detail the wire work. The magnet engineers get their data. The wires were Nb3Sn. The heat was specific. The engineers got data.
doe-osti-3000516-advancing-additive-manu: 3D printing got its AI quality check, and this DOE text scans parts without breaking them. The pages detail the high-speed tests. The manufacturing crew gets its toolkit. The check was nondestructive. The tests were high-speed. The toolkit was crew's.
doe-osti-3002079-advancing-additive-manu: 3D printing got its AI quality check, and this DOE text scans parts without breaking them. The pages detail the high-speed tests. The manufacturing crew gets its toolkit. The check was nondestructive. The tests were high-speed. The toolkit was crew's.

The neutron folks get their data. The deviation was time-of-flight. The data were neutron. The diffractometer was VULCAN. The flight was time.

The chemists get their closeout. The trial was bench-scale. The recipe was sorbent. The sponges were carbon.
doe-osti-3025226-self-healing-cements-wi: Well cement that fixes its own cracks got its DOE toughness upgrade, and this text heals the casing bond. The pages detail the interface results. The geothermal folks get their data. The upgrade was self-healing. The bond was casing.

The climate folks get their data. The structures were engineered. The data were climate. The performance were high. The capture were direct.
doe-osti-3362601-filament-extension-atom: Spray dryers got filament-atomized, and this DOE text loads high solids efficiently. The pages detail the energy findings. The engineers get their data. The systems were energy efficient. The data were engineer. The drying were spray. The solids were high.
lizzie-leigh:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens this story with death on Christmas Day. James Leigh dies as Rochdale's bells ring for morning service. The year is 1836, and his wife Annie keeps vigil. He whispers his forgiveness before his eyes glaze.

Annie begs God to bless him for saying those words. They had been married two and twenty years together. Nineteen of those years passed calm and happy, Gaskell writes. His whispered pardon concerns their absent daughter Lizzie. Milton's famous line framed their married rule of life. He stood as interpreter between God and her, Gaskell writes.
mr-britling-sees-it-through:
H. G. Wells copyrighted this novel in 1916, as the First World War consumed Europe. Its three books chart one village's passage. Book One, Matching's Easy at Ease, shows an American visitor, Mr. Direck, at Mr. Britling's Essex home. Britling expounds, entertains, and soliloquizes while peace still holds.

Book Two is Matching's Easy at War: onlookers, then participants, then the web of the ineffective. Book Three, the testament, ends with Britling writing until sunrise. Wells uses his essayist hero to think through England's shock, grief, and endurance. The novel became his most direct reckoning with the war's cost to ordinary families.
nasa-tm-19650009667-instrumentation-and-:
J C Modlin at Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report on four Nike-Apache sounding rocket flights. The flights were numbered 14.79 UE through 14.82 UE. They were fired from the Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station in India, near the equator.

Modlin documents the flight instrumentation and the flight results in full. The report belongs to a series from the Sounding Rocket Instrumentation Section. Each report kept the engineering data from actual flights in one place. For later teams, that record showed what the telemetry gear did on real launches, not just on the bench.
nasa-tm-19650012066-periodic-wind-compon:
R G Roper and W G Elford presented this March 1965 Goddard paper on winds very high above Earth. At meteor heights, winds cannot be measured with balloons or aircraft. Instead, radio signals bounce off the ionized trails that meteors leave behind. Those reflections reveal how the air up there moves.

Roper and Elford focus on periodic parts of the wind, patterns that repeat with time. Tides in the upper air are one such pattern. Measuring them helped build a picture of a region few instruments could reach. The method turned brief meteor trails into a regular source of data.
nasa-tm-19700013794-a-computer-program-f:
Kenneth C. White of the Ames Research Center wrote this report in April 1970. It describes a computer program for tracing light rays through spacecraft windows. Windows bend light, and crews need to know how much a window shifts what they see.

White wrote the program in FORTRAN IV, a common language of the time. It computes how far each ray is deflected from its first path by the window. The program can handle any type of window, the abstract states, with no restriction on shape. Such a tool helped designers check sight lines for crewed spacecraft.
pebbles-on-the-shore-by-alpha-of-the-plo: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Pebbles on the Shore, the title page, dedication, and contents, with no essay text visible. The title page gives the author as Alpha of the Plough, the pen name of A. G. Gardiner, and dates the book 1916. The contents list familiar essays on letter-writing, reading in bed, cats and dogs, rumour, umbrella morals, the village and the war, and thoughts at fifty.
petronius-satyricon-firebaugh:
Petronius, courtier to the emperor Nero, wrote the Satyricon in the first century. W. C. Firebaugh translated the surviving fragments into complete English form. Only parts of the comic novel remain, centered on books fourteen to sixteen.

Encolpius and his companions drift through southern Italy's low life and pleasures. The vulgar feast of the freedman Trimalchio forms the famous centerpiece. Petronius mocks wealth, taste, and literary pretension with cool amusement. Firebaugh's edition adds the traditional supplementary fragments used to fill gaps. Rude, funny, and broken by time, the Satyricon gives an unmatched view of Roman street level.
poems-by-the-way-love-is-enough: Publisher's catalogue pages for William Morris's collected works open this record, listing the cheaper issue of the library edition of his poetical works in eleven volumes. The listing names the Earthly Paradise in four volumes, the Defence of Guenevere, the Life and Death of Jason. Poems by the Way bound with Love Is Enough, alongside his verse translations of Virgil, Homer, and Beowulf. Prices, formats, and prose romances follow. The pages map Morris's whole output as his publisher sold it, though they carry almost none of the poetry itself.
speed-the-plough:
Thomas Morton wrote Speed the Plough, a comedy in five acts. The Theatre Royal at Covent Garden played it. Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme printed the London book. The text came from the prompt book, by leave of the managers. Remarks by Mrs. Inchbald stand with the play. A front picture dates to 1806. Singleton painted it and Fittler engraved it. It shows Ashfield in Act I, Scene II.

Inchbald praises the play's power to wake curiosity. That feeling, she says, best guards a drama's success. The first two acts pass in fun. Ashfield and his wife are well drawn there. Sir Abel's bent for modern improvements gives just satire. The later acts raise deep interest and keen hope. Both are well paid at the close. The play ranked from its first night with Morton's best. It stands in the first class of modern comedies, she holds.
the-mistletoe-bough:
A story called The Mistletoe Bough, printed in the 1864 Chapman and Hall Tales of All Countries edition, opens with a family argument at Thwaite Hall. Frank Garrow has brought a mistletoe branch home from the Lowther woods. He wants it hung in the dining room on Christmas Eve, as custom allowed kissing beneath it.

His sister Elizabeth begs their mother to refuse, calling the custom mere romping and unsuitable for their guest Miss Holmes. Mrs. Garrow rules against the bough. The narrator muses that kissing had grown less innocent since their grandmothers' day. Frank, eighteen, and Harry, a year younger, tease their sister as a puritan and a fine lady once the decision reaches them.
westward-ho-or-the-voyages-and-adventure:
Charles Kingsley wrote Westward Ho!, a novel of the sea in the reign of Queen Elizabeth. Kingsley dated his dedication February 1855. He gave the book to Sir James Brooke and to Bishop George Selwyn of New Zealand. He praised both men as bold, godly, and selfless in their work.

The hero is Amyas Leigh, a Devon sailor drawn into wars and voyages of the age. Early chapter titles tell of a white bird seen by Mr. Oxenham and of Amyas coming home. Love, hunting, and old Clovelly Court all enter the tale. Readers get high adventure mixed with strong praise for Elizabethan England.
